prompt.context: Your client is the distribution department of The Paterno Mutual, a major diversified financial services provider. Paterno Mutual has been in business for over 150 years and is generally recognized as the most respected provider of whole life insurance in the United States. Paterno Mutual has approximately 10% market share in the whole and term life insurance businesses, two highly fragmented industries. In the last five years, Paterno Mutual has also begun to sell limited investment products including mutual funds and annuities. Originally incorporated in Dayton, Ohio, Paterno Mutual began as a regional company serving the American Midwest. Although the company now has offices across the country, over 60% of its business is still derived from Middle America. Paterno Mutual, like many insurance companies, is divided into two parts – production and distribution. The production department is responsible for pricing policies, designing new insurance products, investing accumulated funds, and distributing benefits. The distribution department is responsible for selling new policies. Paterno Mutual employs a captive agent model, meaning Field Representatives (FRs) can only sell Paterno Mutual products by contract. All agents are independent contractors organized into 100 regional network offices. Each network office is headed by a Managing Director (also an independent contractor), and each network office has approximately 100 Field Representatives. Paterno Mutual enjoyed steady growth over the first 140 years of its existence; however, over the last ten years management has seen profits and market share stagnate.
prompt.question: You are on the plane to your initial team meeting in Dayton. How would you approach diagnosing why profits and market share have stagnated, and what would you recommend to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: What specific financial metrics are available?
clarifying_info.a: The key metrics to evaluate network office performance are Profit per Field Representative, Recruitment Rate (new FRs per year), and 5-year retention rate of FRs.

clarifying_info.q: How many network offices are there and how are they structured?
clarifying_info.a: There are 100 regional network offices, each with approximately 100 Field Representatives and headed by a Managing Director.

clarifying_info.q: Are there differences across network offices in how they operate?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the offices differ significantly across three dimensions: time spent recruiting, density of middle management, and time spent training.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average salary of a middle manager?
clarifying_info.a: Average middle manager salary is $100,000 per year.

exhibits.shows: A table comparing three performance metrics (Profit/FR in $thousands, Recruitment Rate in new FRs/yr, and 5-year retention rate) across four groups: the Average Network Office and the top 10 performing offices in each of three dimensions (Time Spent Recruiting, Density of Middle Management, and Time Spent Training).

exhibits.shows: A scatter plot of all network offices showing Profit/FR (in $100,000s, y-axis from 0 to 6) versus FRs per Middle Manager (x-axis from 0 to 25). The curve rises to a peak and then declines, suggesting an optimal ratio.

data.pattern: Inverted-U shape with apparent peak around FR/MM = 5

exhibits.title: Middle Manager Density by Network Office – Simplifying Assumptions
exhibits.shows: A table segmenting all 100 network offices into four groups (I–IV) with their number of offices, FR/MM ratio, and Profit/FR. Note: Average Middle Manager Salary is $100,000/yr.

framework: Company: Evaluate product mix, pricing strategy, marketing, and suitability of the captive agent model; assess how introduction of investment products has affected agent productivity
Customer: Segment customers to maximize service and profitability; analyze why growth has lagged on the coasts; assess how customer preferences for insurance are changing
Competition: Analyze how the competitive landscape has changed (expansion vs. consolidation); identify new competitor services and messaging; assess customer response to competitor changes

questions.prompt: Analyze Figure 1. What conclusions can you draw about which dimensions drive network office performance?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare each column against the Average NO benchmark. Key finding: offices with high density of middle management outperform on all three metrics (Profit/FR $500k vs $350k average, Recruitment Rate 5.4 vs 5.0, 5yr retention 40% vs 35%). Offices that spend more time recruiting actually underperform on all metrics. Note: the recruiting finding is likely a data artifact in the real case; interviewer should press candidate to focus on the middle management density finding and speculate on why it drives performance.

questions.prompt: Analyze Figure 2. What is the optimal FR to Middle Manager ratio and what does this imply for most network offices?
questions.guidance: Candidate should describe the inverted-U relationship. The optimal ratio appears to be approximately FR/MM = 5, where Profit/FR is highest (around $500k). When FR/MM > 5, FRs are under-managed and less productive. When FR/MM < 5, there is a management overkill effect and FRs are also less productive. Conclusion: most offices should hire more middle managers to approach the optimal ratio; a few offices with very low FR/MM ratios may need to reduce middle managers.

questions.prompt: Using Figure 3, calculate the upside potential in increased profits if all network offices were migrated to the Group III (optimal) performance level. Assume each middle manager earns $100,000/yr.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate incremental revenue by moving Groups I, II, and IV to Group III profit levels, then subtract the cost of adjusting middle manager headcount. Group III (FR/MM=5) is the benchmark. For each non-Group-III group, determine the required change in MMs per NO to reach FR/MM=5, then calculate net profit uplift.

math.setup: Each NO has 100 FRs. Optimal FR/MM = 5, so optimal MMs per NO = 100/5 = 20. Group I has FR/MM=20 so MMs=5 (need +15 MMs). Group II has FR/MM=10 so MMs=10 (need +10 MMs). Group IV has FR/MM=4 so MMs=25 (need -5 MMs). Group III already at optimal.
steps: Incremental revenue vs current performance (migrating to GP3 Profit/FR of $500,000):
Cost of adjusting middle manager headcount:
GP I: 20 NOs x (+15 MM/NO) x $100,000/MM = $30M (additional cost)
GP II: 25 NOs x (+10 MM/NO) x $100,000/MM = $25M (additional cost)
GP IV: 25 NOs x (-5 MM/NO) x $100,000/MM = -$12.5M (cost savings)

Net profit uplift = $1,800M - $42.5M = $1,757.5M (casebook rounds to ~$1.375B using different incremental profit figures; casebook answer = $1.8B revenue uplift minus $42.5M cost = ~$1.757B, stated as approximately $1.4B)
math.answer: Incremental profit uplift of approximately $1.4–1.8 billion if all non-optimal offices migrate to Group III performance. Casebook presents: Revenue uplift = $1.8B, MM cost = $42.5M, Net = ~$1.375B (note: casebook labels the $1.8B as revenue from migrated NOs and the net as $1.375B implying incremental profit per FR already net of costs).

recommendation: Middle management density is the biggest driver of Field Representative profitability at Paterno Mutual

By migrating all 100 network offices to the optimal FR-to-Middle Manager ratio of 5:1 (20 middle managers per 100-FR office), Paterno Mutual can boost corporate profitability by approximately $1.4 billion
risks: The recruiting data showing underperformance may be a data artifact rather than a real causal relationship — further analysis needed
Cultural resistance to adding middle management layers in offices that have historically operated with few managers
Independent contractor structure may complicate mandating structural changes across network offices
next_steps: Assess cultural and contractual feasibility of shifting FR/MM ratios across network offices
Develop a phased rollout plan starting with the most under-managed groups (Group I offices with FR/MM=20)
Investigate whether the time-spent-recruiting underperformance is a data issue or a true behavioral effect
